VI-15 The partridge is cold, but still the domestic hen is colder than the partridge, and it has an imperfection in itself, and the partridge is also more unstable than the domestic hen. Its flesh is also not firm but fragile, because it is neither entirely of air nor entirely of earth; and when eaten it does not do much harm to the healthy, but it is of no use to the weak, because it prepares slime in their stomachs. Take also its gall, and mix it with old arvine [fat], and on whose skin lice grow outwardly from the sweat of the flesh, let him anoint himself with it often, and it passes through his skin, and purifies the sweat, so that the lice grow no more. For the gall of the same bird is filled with both the bitter and sweet juice of herbs, and therefore its bitterness and coldness, tempered with the heat of the arvine, which also resists lice, mortifies those who grow outwardly from the sweat of the flesh, but not those who are inwardly from the arvine of man, because the same bird does not have the full perfection of good air, as has been foretold. But even if lice grow inwardly from the arvine, then this anointing will not be of any use. But the sweat of the liver of a man does not prepare lice, but the sweat that is from his arvine, and also to some extent the sweat of the lungs, which is bitter, and yet this anointing is of no use. But the rest that is in it will not be of much use as medicines.

VI-16 Birkhun has almost the same nature as rephun, except that the flesh of birkhunes is better and healthier to eat than the flesh of rephunes, because it is more exposed to the air than the partridge. For crabs grow strongly in those men who have in themselves that air, from which many hairs grow in those men who are of a useless and moist air.
